topology: Declared linear type-2 second-order CDR teaching loop.
planes: Input phase, recovered phase and residual phase at the same time; phase measured in UI.

evidence.provenance: First-principles boundary conditions, linear circuit laws or the declared teaching-loop equation; no measured or licensed data.

checks.derivation: Input is a sine with zero phase at t=0.
At f=fn and ζ=.5, H=1−j. A .4 UI peak-to-peak sine has .2 UI amplitude; the quadrature term at t=0 is −.2 UI.
At a quarter period, sin=1 and cos=0; Re(H)=1 gives .2 UI.
Input and recovered phase coincide at a quarter period in this example.

lesson.prediction: If the recovered phase amplitude exceeds the input amplitude, can the residual still be found by subtracting magnitudes?
lesson.experiment: Open the scenario, keep its network and stimulus fixed, and inspect the stated observation. Compare with the derived answer before changing one variable.
lesson.explanation: No. At f=fn the real part of the denominator vanishes; the declared loop reduces to H=1−j/(2ζ). At ζ=.5 the residual transfer is j, so the phase relation determines instantaneous error.
lesson.transferQuestion: Does this frequency equal the closed-loop −3 dB bandwidth?
lesson.answer: No. It is the natural frequency of the declared denominator; the closed-loop bandwidth depends on damping and the numerator.

limitations: Steady-state linear teaching loop, not acquisition, cycle slips, noise, or a BER-qualified tolerance mask.
Peak-to-peak input amplitude is twice its sine amplitude.
Quarter-period sample is checked against its exported time coordinate.
stimulus: Steady-state sinusoidal input phase, 0.4 UI peak-to-peak at 4 MHz.
